words.definition: Concerned with ideas and principles rather than practical application or real-world use.
words.example: Her knowledge of engines was purely theoretical—she had never actually taken one apart.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'theory' hiding inside it: THEORY-etical describes something living in ideas, not in the workshop.

words.definition: To watch or notice something carefully in order to learn about it.
words.example: The scientists sat motionless for hours to observe how the wolves hunted at dusk.
words.mnemonic: 'ob-SERVE': a good waiter serves you by carefully watching your table's every need.

words.definition: The act of watching something closely, or a remark about what was noticed.
words.example: After a week of quiet observation, the birdwatcher knew exactly which flowers the hummingbirds preferred.
words.mnemonic: Picture an 'observation deck'—the platform you stand on just to watch the view below.

words.definition: To examine something in detail by breaking it into separate parts.
words.example: The coach stayed up late to analyze the game footage frame by frame.
words.mnemonic: Ends in '-lyze', like 'lysis'—to split apart; you split a thing into pieces to study it.

words.definition: A detailed examination of the separate parts of something to understand it.
words.example: The lab's analysis of the tap water revealed alarming traces of lead.
words.mnemonic: Ends in '-lysis' like dialysis, where blood is broken down and filtered part by part.

words.definition: To combine separate elements into a single unified whole.
words.example: Plants synthesize sugar from nothing more than sunlight, water, and air.
words.mnemonic: 'syn-' means together (like synchronize); a synth combines many tones into one sound.

words.definition: The combining of separate parts into a unified whole.
words.example: Her essay was a clever synthesis of ideas borrowed from three rival philosophers.
words.mnemonic: 'syn-' = together; think of a synthesizer fusing many notes into one blended sound.

words.definition: A conclusion reached by reasoning logically from known facts or general rules.
words.example: From the muddy boots and dripping umbrella, the detective made the deduction that it was raining.
words.mnemonic: 'de-' (down) + 'duce' (lead): you are led down from clues to a conclusion, Sherlock-style.

words.definition: The relationship in which one event directly produces or brings about another.
words.example: The study found a link between coffee and long life, but never proved causation.
words.mnemonic: It's 'cause' + '-ation': the machinery by which one thing actually makes another happen.

words.definition: A factor or quantity that can change within an experiment or situation.
words.example: In the experiment, temperature was the one variable the students were allowed to adjust.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'vary-able'—a thing that is able to vary, shifting from value to value.

words.definition: To copy or repeat something exactly.
words.example: Three other labs tried to replicate the experiment but kept getting different results.
words.mnemonic: 're-' (again) + '-plicate' (fold, as in duplicate): to fold out another identical copy.

words.definition: The quality of a result being obtainable again under the same conditions.
words.example: The findings lacked reproducibility, since no other team could get the same outcome twice.
words.mnemonic: Break it up: 're-produce-ibility'—the ability to produce the very same thing again.

words.definition: The quality of being logically sound, well-founded, and defensible.
words.example: The lawyer attacked the validity of the confession because it had been coerced.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'validus' (strong); like a 'valid' ticket, it stands up strongly to a challenge.

words.definition: The quality of being consistently trustworthy and dependable over time.
words.example: The old truck's reliability meant it started every winter morning without fail for a decade.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'rely' inside it: the ability of something you can rely on again and again.

words.definition: To measure or express something as a number or amount.
words.example: It's hard to quantify just how much joy the new puppy brought the family.
words.mnemonic: 'quant-' (how much, as in quantity) + '-ify' (to make): to put an exact number on it.

words.definition: To adjust a measuring instrument so its readings are accurate against a known standard.
words.example: Before the experiment, she carefully calibrated the thermometer against a block of melting ice.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'caliper' — picture a lab tech fine-tuning a machine with calipers until it's exactly right.

words.definition: To measure or judge the size, amount, or nature of something.
words.example: He glanced around the room to gauge how the audience was reacting to his speech.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'cage'; picture a fuel gauge you read to judge how much is left in the tank.

words.definition: To form a rough judgment of a value, size, or cost without exact measurement.
words.example: The contractor estimated that the repairs would take about three weeks.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'est.' — the abbreviation you scribble beside a number when it's only a ballpark guess.

words.definition: To come close to a value or quality without being exactly correct.
words.example: The model's prediction approximates the real temperature to within a degree or two.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'proxim-' as in 'proximity' — being near the mark but not landing on it.

words.definition: Facts or signs that help prove whether something is true or false.
words.example: The muddy footprints by the door were the only evidence that someone had slipped inside.
words.mnemonic: Say 'it is e-VIDENT' — evidence is what makes a truth plainly visible.

words.definition: To show that something is definitely true or correct.
words.example: A second blood test confirmed the original diagnosis.
words.mnemonic: Con-FIRM — to make a shaky idea 'firm' and settled, no longer in doubt.

words.definition: To prove a statement wrong, or to tamper with records dishonestly.
words.example: The scientist designed an experiment that could, in principle, falsify her own hypothesis.
words.mnemonic: 'False' + '-ify' — to make-into or expose-as false.

words.definition: To carefully consider something in order to judge its value, quality, or importance.
words.example: The teacher paused to assess whether the class had really grasped the lesson.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a session' — sit in session and weigh the facts before deciding.

words.definition: To judge the worth, amount, or significance of something after careful thought.
words.example: Reviewers will evaluate each grant proposal on originality and feasibility.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'value' — to e-VALU-ate is literally to find the value of something.

words.definition: To judge the quality or monetary worth of something, often officially.
words.example: A jeweler appraised the ring at twice what she had paid for it.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-PRICE' inside it — to appraise is to set a price on something's worth.

words.definition: To explain or decide the meaning of something, or to translate between languages.
words.example: It was hard to interpret her silence — was it anger, or simply exhaustion?
words.mnemonic: 'Inter-' (between) + 'pret' — you go between the lines and carry the meaning out.

words.definition: To understand a word, action, or situation in a particular way.
words.example: Please don't construe my silence as agreement; I just had nothing to add.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'construct' a view — you build the meaning you take from something.

words.definition: To arrange things into groups based on shared features.
words.example: Biologists classify the newly discovered insect among the beetles.
words.mnemonic: Put into a 'class' — like sorting students into the right classroom.

words.definition: To place items into defined classes according to their type or purpose.
words.example: The app lets you categorize expenses as essentials, savings, or treats.
words.mnemonic: Holds 'category' — to drop each thing into its proper category bin.

words.definition: Done according to a fixed, organized plan or method rather than at random.
words.example: Her systematic search of the attic, box by box, finally turned up the old letters.
words.mnemonic: Follows a 'system' — step by step, nothing left to chance.

words.definition: Following an ordered, step-by-step system with careful attention to detail.
words.example: She unpacked every box in a methodical order, labeling each one before opening the next.
words.mnemonic: METHODical — someone who always follows a METHOD, one deliberate step after another.

words.definition: Extremely thorough, careful, and demanding in meeting strict standards.
words.example: Every sample went through rigorous testing before the team dared to publish a result.
words.mnemonic: Rigor = rigid; RIGOROUS rules are stiff and unbending, like a drill sergeant who won't relax them.

words.definition: Exact and clearly defined, with no vagueness or error.
words.example: Give me the precise time — not 'around noon,' but exactly 12:03.
words.mnemonic: PRE-CISE sounds like 'pre-scissors': an exact, clean cut with no ragged edges.

words.definition: Correct and free from mistakes; matching the true value.
words.example: The new scale is so accurate it registers a single grain of rice.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'accuratus' (done with care) — think 'a cure' that works exactly, hitting the target right.

words.definition: Coming before the main part, as preparation or introduction.
words.example: The preliminary sketches were drawn weeks before the artist touched the final canvas.
words.mnemonic: PRE- (before) + 'limin' (Latin limen, threshold): what happens before you cross the threshold.

words.definition: Hard to believe; unlikely to be true.
words.example: His excuse — that aliens ate his homework — was completely implausible.
words.mnemonic: IM- (not) + 'plausible' (from Latin plaudere, to applaud): a tale so unbelievable you can't applaud it.

words.definition: Different from what is normal or expected; irregular.
words.example: The thermometer showed an anomalous spike no one could explain on such a cold day.
words.mnemonic: A-NOMAL-ous: 'a' (not) plus 'nomal,' which sounds like NORMAL — so, not normal.

words.definition: Staying the same over time; steady and free of contradiction.
words.example: Her grades were consistent all year — never a surprise, high or low.
words.mnemonic: CON- (with) + 'sist' (Latin sistere, to stand): parts that stand together and agree.

words.definition: Not staying the same; changeable or self-contradictory.
words.example: His story was inconsistent — the times he gave kept shifting with each retelling.
words.mnemonic: IN- (not) + consistent: the parts refuse to stand together, so they don't hold.

words.definition: A value or person sitting far away from all the others in a group.
words.example: In a class of average scores, her perfect 100 was a clear outlier.
words.mnemonic: OUT + LIE: it lies OUTside the pack, way off from where everyone else sits.

words.definition: An observable event or fact, especially one that is remarkable.
words.example: The northern lights are a phenomenon travelers cross the globe to witness.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'phainein' (to show) — something that shows itself, appearing for all to see.

words.definition: A system of parts working together, or the way a process operates.
words.example: Scientists finally uncovered the mechanism by which the drug lowers blood pressure.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'machine' inside MECHANISM — picture the gears and inner workings that make it run.

words.definition: An established series of steps for doing something.
words.example: The nurse followed the emergency procedure exactly, step by careful step.
words.mnemonic: PROCEED + -ure: it spells out how you proceed from one action to the next.

words.definition: The official rules for how something should be done or handled.
words.example: Hospital protocol requires two nurses to verify the dosage before any injection.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'protos' (first) + 'kolla' (glue): the first sheet glued to a document, laying down the rules.

words.definition: A typical model or pattern of thinking that shapes how people understand something.
words.example: Einstein's ideas created a new paradigm that replaced Newton's view of the universe.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'para' (beside) + 'deigma' (example): a model set beside you to copy — say it 'PAIR-a-dime.'

words.definition: A supporting structure of ideas or rules used to organize a plan or system.
words.example: Before writing any code, the team agreed on a framework for how the modules would talk to each other.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'frame' + 'work' — the wooden frame workers raise before any walls go up.

words.definition: To build or form something by putting parts together.
words.example: Engineers will construct the bridge from prefabricated steel sections shipped overnight.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + Latin 'struere' (to build) — the same root gives us 'structure.'

words.definition: A general idea formed apart from any specific real object or event.
words.example: To a hungry child, freedom is just an abstraction; a warm meal is not.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'abstrahere' = to draw away — an idea drawn away from the physical thing.

words.definition: Existing as a real, physical thing that can be touched or clearly seen.
words.example: Stop giving me vague promises and hand me a concrete plan with actual dates.
words.mnemonic: Picture the gray building material — solid, hard, and right there under your feet.

words.definition: Not swayed by strong emotion; calm and fair when judging.
words.example: The judge delivered a dispassionate ruling, unmoved by the crowd's shouting.
words.mnemonic: dis- (without) + passionate — literally without the heat of feeling.

words.definition: Having no personal stake, and therefore able to judge fairly.
words.example: We asked a disinterested neighbor to settle the argument, since neither of us could be trusted to be fair.
words.mnemonic: A referee is dis-interested — no money riding on either team, so his calls stay fair.

words.definition: Free from prejudice; treating every side equally.
words.example: A good scientist reports unbiased results even when they disprove her own theory.
words.mnemonic: un- (not) + bias — the arrow isn't tilted toward one side.

words.definition: Following clear reasoning; sensible and internally consistent.
words.example: It's the only logical conclusion: if the door was bolted from inside, no intruder came through it.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'logos' (reason) — a step-by-step path where each step earns the next.

words.definition: To form ideas explaining why something happens, often before proof exists.
words.example: Detectives began to theorize that the fire had been set deliberately.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'theoria' (a viewing) — you stage an explanation in your mind before checking the facts.

words.definition: To draw one broad conclusion from only a few specific cases.
words.example: You can't generalize about an entire country after visiting a single city.
words.mnemonic: A 'general' commands the whole army, not one soldier — you sweep across everything at once.

words.definition: To give or allow something formally, usually after a request.
words.example: The king agreed to grant the villagers the right to farm his land.
words.mnemonic: Hear the genie: 'Your wish is granted' — he hands the thing over.

words.definition: To improve something through small, careful changes that remove flaws.
words.example: After the rough first draft, she spent a week polishing and working to refine every paragraph.
words.mnemonic: re- (again) + 'fine' — make it fine again, buffing out the rough spots.

words.definition: To change or update a piece of work after looking it over again.
words.example: The editor asked me to revise the ending because it felt rushed.
words.mnemonic: re- (again) + Latin 'videre' (to see) — to see it again and fix what's wrong.

words.definition: To make small changes to a text or law in order to improve it.
words.example: Congress voted to amend the bill by adding two new clauses.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'a-mend' — you mend, or patch, a document.

words.definition: To combine separate parts into one unified whole.
words.example: The new software helps integrate sales and shipping data onto a single dashboard.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'integer' (whole) — the same root as a whole number; you make the pieces whole together.

words.definition: To give a short version of something, covering only its most important points.
words.example: After the two-hour meeting, she summarized the outcome in three quick bullet points.
words.mnemonic: Sum + marize — you add up the 'sum' of the main ideas and leave the rest out.

words.definition: To express someone else's idea again in your own words while keeping the meaning.
words.example: Rather than quote the professor directly, he paraphrased her argument in simpler terms.
words.mnemonic: 'para' (beside) + 'phrase' — you set a fresh phrase beside the original one.

words.definition: To say or do something again, usually to make a point unmistakably clear.
words.example: The coach reiterated the safety rules before letting anyone touch the equipment.
words.mnemonic: 're' (again) + 'iterate' (loop through) — to run through it one more time.

words.definition: To give special importance or attention to something in speech or writing.
words.example: She emphasized the deadline by writing it in red on the board.
words.mnemonic: Say 'em-PHA-size' — you make one part big and loud so it stands out.

words.definition: To make a feature or quality more noticeable or prominent.
words.example: The tailored jacket accentuated his broad shoulders.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'accent' — an accent mark makes one syllable pop.

words.definition: To serve as a clear, typical instance that shows what something is like.
words.example: Her calm response under pressure exemplified true professionalism.
words.mnemonic: 'exempl-' like 'example' + '-ify' (to make) — to turn into a model case.

words.definition: To be a perfect representation of a particular quality or type.
words.example: With his tireless generosity, he epitomized what it means to be a good neighbor.
words.mnemonic: From 'epitome' — the flawless, boiled-down model of a thing.

words.definition: To describe the distinctive qualities of something, or be a typical feature of it.
words.example: Critics characterized the film as slow but deeply moving.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'character' — you sketch the traits, the character, of something.

words.definition: A point or opinion that a person strongly puts forward as true in an argument.
words.example: Her central contention was that the policy would hurt small businesses.
words.mnemonic: 'contend' + '-tion' — a contention is exactly what you contend for.

words.definition: Something suggested or made likely without being directly stated.
words.example: He said nothing rude, but the implication of his cold silence was clear.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'plicare' (to fold) — a meaning folded in rather than spoken aloud.

words.definition: To form the hidden basis or foundation of something more visible.
words.example: A deep anxiety about failure seemed to underlie his relentless need to win every argument.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: 'under' + 'lie' — the cause that literally lies under the surface of what you see.
